exercise.title: What does a finite difference remember?

statement.p: From a list of positions at equally spaced times we form differences s_j-s_{j-1}. In your own words, what physical quantity do those differences record, and why is no limiting process required yet?

hint.p: On a genuine step of fixed length, the change is exact. Limits appear only when the step itself is trying to shrink to an instant.

subsection.p: So even before limits, we see the two directions of calculus:
and

But real motion is usually not made of perfect steps. A car does not hold one exact velocity for a while, jump instantly to another, and hold that forever. Its velocity changes while the clock is running.
For a changing velocity, rectangles are no longer exact. They become estimates. The natural response is to use shorter intervals, then shorter ones still.
That is where limits enter.

exercise.title: How can calculus exist before limits?

statement.p: Finite differences go from position to change; finite sums go from change back to position. In your own words, why is that already the two-direction story of calculus, and what can this discrete version not yet handle?

hint.p: The inverse relationship does not require infinitely small steps. It fails to be exact as soon as the velocity changes inside a step rather than only at the endpoints.
